"Stalk" has three distinct meanings. They are different enough that you need to learn each one separately, but you'll notice a quiet thread connecting them all: deliberate, focused movement or attention.
Meaning 1: To follow or spy on someone obsessively (and usually secretly)

This is the most important and widely used meaning today.

When someone stalks another person, they follow them, watch them, or track their activities repeatedly — in a way that is unwanted, intrusive, and often frightening. The person doing it is called a stalker.

The key ideas packed into this meaning:

  • It's persistent — it happens again and again, not just once.
  • It's unwanted — the person being stalked has not agreed to this attention.
  • It's often secret or hidden — the stalker tries not to be noticed.
  • It causes fear or distress to the victim.
  • It is considered a crime in most countries.

Examples:

  • "He stalked his ex-girlfriend for months, showing up wherever she went."
  • "The celebrity was stalked by a fan who knew her daily schedule."

This doesn't only happen in person. In the modern world, stalking also happens online, and this is called cyberstalking:

  • Obsessively monitoring someone's social media profiles
  • Tracking their location through apps without their knowledge
  • Sending repeated unwanted messages

Informal / Lighter Use:
In casual conversation among friends, people sometimes use "stalk" in a much lighter, joking way — meaning to look someone up on social media out of curiosity:

  • "I totally stalked his Instagram profile last night."

This informal use is harmless and common, but understand that the serious meaning carries real weight and describes actual criminal behaviour.
Meaning 2: To hunt or pursue prey by moving slowly and silently

This meaning comes from the world of hunting and the animal kingdom.

When a predator or a hunter stalks its prey, it moves toward it very slowly, quietly, and carefully — trying not to make a sound or be seen — so it can get close enough to catch it.

The key ideas here:

  • The movement is slow and deliberate.
  • The goal is to get close without being detected.
  • There is a clear hunter and a target (prey).

Examples:

  • "The lion stalked the zebra through the tall grass for several minutes before pouncing."
  • "The hunter stalked the deer silently through the forest."
  • "The cat stalked the mouse across the kitchen floor."

This is deeply instinctive behaviour — you'll see it in nature documentaries constantly. Notice how the lion crouches low, moves one careful step at a time, freezes when the prey looks up — that entire process is "stalking."
Meaning 3: To walk in a stiff, proud, or angry manner

This meaning describes a way of walking — specifically, walking with long, stiff, deliberate steps that signals a strong emotion, usually anger, irritation, or contempt.

When someone stalks out of a room or stalks off, they are usually expressing that they are upset or offended. It's a dramatic, purposeful walk — not casual or relaxed.

The key ideas:

  • The steps are long and stiff.
  • The body language is tense and deliberate.
  • It usually communicates anger, pride, or disapproval.
  • It is often followed by a direction: stalk off, stalk out, stalk away, stalk past.

Examples:

  • "After the argument, she stalked out of the room and slammed the door."
  • "He stalked off in anger when no one listened to him."
  • "The offended guest stalked past the host without saying a word."

Think of it like this: a normal person walks out of a room. An angry or deeply offended person stalks out of it — with purpose, tension, and attitude in every step.

Even though these three meanings seem very different on the surface, notice the common thread running through all of them:

In every case, the movement or attention is slow, deliberate, focused, and intense.

  • The predator moves with controlled, focused intensity toward its prey.
  • The stalker watches with obsessive, locked-in focus on their target.
  • The angry person walks with rigid, deliberate intensity out of a situation.

None of these are casual, relaxed, or accidental. "Stalk" always suggests something purposeful and charged with intensity.

One Last Thing: Meaning by Context

Because "stalk" has three meanings, context always tells you which one is meant:

  • If the subject is a person targeting another person in everyday life → obsessive following.
  • If the subject is an animal or hunter → silent hunting pursuit.
  • If someone is described as stalking out/off/away/past → angry walking.

You will almost never be confused if you pay attention to these context clues.
